headline: High-risk shared-bus and broad-egress pairing: OpenHands can write/egress while Pipecat routes shared conversation state to third-party services.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can read/write files and use MCP, so it may ingest attacker-controlled content from its runtime. Pipecat uses a shared bus and shared conversation state, creating a plausible bridge if outputs are forwarded between them. No direct documented parser bridge is shown, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF OpenHands reads Pipecat-delivered text as instructions without sanitization, injection is possible.
IF both agents are connected through a shared bus or mounted volume, prompt content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Disable automatic forwarding of Pipecat messages into OpenHands prompts.
Add a strict allowlist for MCP tools exposed to OpenHands.
Insert a content sanitizer that strips instruction-like text before handoff.
Use separate runtimes or buses for the two agents.
Log and review any cross-agent message relay for prompt-like payloads.

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands touches mounted files and can egress broadly; Pipecat handles text, audio, video, and conversation state on a shared bus. If the pair shares a workspace or bus, sensitive runtime files or conversation data can flow into third-party APIs through Pipecat or OpenHands. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so this remains medium rather than high.
conditions: IF the two agents share a mounted volume or message bus, data can cross between them.
IF Pipecat is configured with external STT/LLM/TTS services, conversation content leaves the local boundary.
IF OpenHands is given secrets in mounted files, those files may be read and transmitted onward.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of any shared volume.
Route Pipecat through local-only providers where possible.
Separate the agents onto distinct workspaces or buses.
Disable broad egress for OpenHands unless needed.
Review provider settings for any automatic transcript upload.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands has filesystem write and git-state modification; Pipecat is a shared-bus framework that can run across processes and machines. If both are pointed at the same mutable workspace or repo, concurrent writes or state updates can conflict. The profiles do not confirm a shared directory, so the risk is plausible but not proven.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF OpenHands modifies git state while Pipecat or its plugins also mutate the repo, conflicts can arise.
IF no external locking is present, concurrent updates may race.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Use a lock file around any shared repo writes.
Disable git writes in OpenHands when Pipecat is active.
Serialize state updates through one orchestrator.
Snapshot the workspace before concurrent runs.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can generate code or actions from its agent loop, while Pipecat can carry conversation state on a shared bus. If Pipecat forwards OpenHands output into downstream speech or action pipelines without verification, errors can cascade into user-facing responses or tool actions. No direct evidence of such a pipeline is provided, so medium is the cautious choice.
conditions: IF Pipecat treats OpenHands output as authoritative, mistakes propagate downstream.
IF OpenHands emits unverified facts that Pipecat renders to users, the error becomes user-visible.
IF either agent triggers actions from the other's output, the cascade widens.
mitigations: Add a verification step before Pipecat relays OpenHands output.
Require human approval for any action derived from OpenHands text.
Tag OpenHands outputs as untrusted provenance.
Limit Pipecat to summarizing, not executing, cross-agent content.
Record source attribution on every forwarded message.

E_compliance.rationale: OpenHands explicitly handles model-provider API keys and runtime-mounted files, while Pipecat commonly sends audio/text to external STT/LLM/TTS services. If regulated or sensitive data enters the pair, residency and retention obligations can diverge across those third-party providers. The profiles do not specify a concrete jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed through external Pipecat providers, residency/retention obligations may be triggered.
IF OpenHands mounts sensitive files while Pipecat logs transcripts, compliance scope expands.
IF the deployment requires HIPAA/GDPR controls, provider selection becomes material.
mitigations: Restrict both agents to non-sensitive data.
Choose providers with documented retention and residency terms.
Disable transcript logging where possible.
Keep a written data-flow map for the pair.
Review whether any regulated data is entering mounted files or conversations.
